subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: talking with parents and weighing their concerns [Action]
passage: “Honestly, nobody believes me when I say I didn't argue.” I'm Sabina, and last month a students' march was planned over leaked exam papers. My father, Wasim, said no at once: board prep, crowds, all of it. Instead of shouting, I asked him to tell me every single thing he was scared of. He listed three: getting hurt, losing revision time, being filmed. Then I told him why it mattered, that my cousin lost a whole year because of the leak. Ammi sat down and listened as well. In the end we made a deal. I wouldn't go to the march itself. I'd make posters with the school group at home on Saturday and join the small signature table outside our colony gate. Abbu even carried the posters out. Part of me still wanted to be there, but it felt fair.

qa.q: What three things was Wasim scared of?
qa.a: Getting hurt, losing revision time and being filmed.

qa.q: What might Sabina have been feeling about the deal at the end?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: part of Sabina still wanted to be at the march, but the outcome felt fair because both sides had been heard.

qa.q: What could Sabina try if the parents had refused any kind of taking part, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could write a letter or speak at a school forum from home, since it voices the concern while keeping the family's trust.

qa.q: How does the deal look to Wasim?
qa.a: His worries about safety and revision were listened to and answered, so he could accept a smaller way of taking part and even help carry the posters.

grounding: A teen listens to parents' worries, explains why the issue matters and agrees a limited form of participation.

passage:
I'm Sumit, and I was in the next room when my cousin Manjula brought up the farmers' march with her parents. She's in Class 11 and had been talking about it all week.

Her father's voice went up first. "Board prep year, and you want to spend a Sunday in a crowd?" Her mother said quietly, "What if something goes wrong?"

Manjula didn't argue back straight away. She listened. Then she said, "I know you're worried. But my friend's family farms, and this matters to them. I'm not asking to go alone."

They talked for almost an hour. I heard numbers, times, names of streets.

In the end, they agreed: she wouldn't go to the march, but she'd help at the peaceful information stall outside the temple that morning, with her mother nearby, and be home by twelve to study.

When she came out, she didn't look like she'd lost. I'm not sure how she felt, but she looked settled.

qa.q: Where would Manjula help instead of the march?
qa.a: At the peaceful information stall outside the temple that morning.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling when she didn't argue back at first?
qa.a: She may have felt frustrated but determined to stay calm, wanting her parents to feel heard before explaining why the issue mattered.

qa.q: What else could Manjula and her parents try if a similar event comes up?
qa.a: They could agree on a simple checklist, like who organises it, where and when, and which adult goes, so the talk starts from facts rather than fear.

qa.q: How did the evening look to Sumit from the next room?
qa.a: Sumit heard raised voices turn into a long, practical talk and saw Manjula come out looking settled, though Sumit can't be sure how she felt.

grounding: An observer describes a teen listening to parents' worries about safety and exams, explaining why an issue matters and agreeing on a form of participation that respects both views.

passage:
Day 1, a Friday: Sangeeta asked her parents at dinner if she could join Sunday's march for a new girls' toilet block at the government school. Her father put his spoon down. "Crowds are not safe. And your exams are in three weeks." Her mother nodded. Sangeeta's cheeks burned. She went to her room and slammed the door.

Day 2, Saturday: She came down calmer. "Can we talk properly?" she asked. She listened first. Her father said he'd seen a peaceful march turn tense years ago. Her mother worried about lost study hours. Then Sangeeta explained that her friend Chandrika's little sister had to go home to use a toilet.

Day 3, Sunday: They'd agreed on a middle way. Sangeeta and her mother collected signatures at the colony gate for an hour, and her father drove the petition to the organisers. She studied that afternoon.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel on day 1 when her father refused?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed, her cheeks burning, and slammed the door.

qa.q: What else could Sangeeta do to stay involved without going to crowded events?
qa.a: She could write to the school management committee or the local councillor, adding a student's voice to the petition in a lawful way.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's father see the Sunday arrangement?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and respected, since his safety worry was heard and he could still help by driving the petition to the organisers.

grounding: Shows a teen listening to parents' worries about safety and exams, explaining why the issue matters, and agreeing together on a form of participation that respects both.
